ELK for Spring Boot microservices

Centralized logging with Elasticsearch, Logstash and Kibana, run locally in Docker for api-gateway, order-service and inventory-service.

1. The big picture

Each microservice writes its own rolling log file. Logstash keeps reading those files, turns each raw line into structured fields, and sends it to Elasticsearch, which indexes it. Kibana then lets you search and chart that data.

Spring servicesgateway, order, inventory
Log fileslogs/<service>/*.log
Logstashtail, parse, route
Elasticsearchindex, query, aggregate
Kibanasearch, dashboards
About "Heartbeat": the log shipper in the Elastic family is Filebeat (Heartbeat is a different tool for uptime checks). In your current setup there is no Filebeat at all: Logstash itself tails the files through its file input, which is the "continuous polling". Port 5044 (Beats input) is reserved for a future Filebeat and is unused today.

2. The three services

Elasticsearch

Stores and searches. A NoSQL, JSON document store built on an inverted index, so full-text search and filters on millions of log lines return in milliseconds.

Core terms: a document is one log event, an index is a collection of documents, and aggregations (counts, averages, group-by) power charts.

Here: port 9200, daily indexes named spring-logs-YYYY.MM.dd, security enabled.

Logstash

Collects and transforms. A pipeline with three stages: input (where events come from), filter (parse and clean), output (where they go).

It turns a text line into fields such as level, thread, trace_context, service and log_message.

Here: reads /logs (your logs folder, mounted read-only), monitoring API on 9600.

Kibana

Shows it. The web UI on top of Elasticsearch: Discover for searching, Lens/Visualize for charts, Dashboards for combined views, Dev Tools for raw API calls.

It holds no logs itself; it only queries Elasticsearch.

Here: http://localhost:5601, sign in as elastic.

3. Step 1: make the services log in a standard format

Every service uses the same logback-spring.xml, so Logstash can parse all of them with one rule. The pattern is the contract between your apps and Logstash:

%d{dd-MM-yyyy HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] [%X{traceId}-%X{spanId}] %-5level ${applicationName}-%logger{36}.%M - %msg%n

A real line from order-service looks like this:

04-10-2026 00:11:27.972 [http-nio-9020-exec-1] [6ac14c577f44c67ee28cde25086193d3-3401c4c7f8570e16] INFO order-service-c.u.o.service.OrderService.createOrder - Creating new order
  • applicationName comes from spring.application.name, so each line carries its service name.
  • traceId and spanId are filled in by tracing (the MDC). The same traceId follows one request across gateway, order and inventory. Outside a request the field shows [-].
  • A RollingFileAppender writes logs/${applicationName}/application-yyyy-MM-dd.N.log, rolling daily or at 10 MB and keeping 30 days. This is the folder Logstash reads.

4. Step 2: start the stack with Docker

All commands run from the repository root in PowerShell.

Create credentials

Copy-Item elk\.env.example elk\.env
notepad elk\.env
ELASTIC_PASSWORD='your-elastic-user-password'
KIBANA_SYSTEM_PASSWORD='your-kibana_system-password'

Never commit .env. Quote passwords that contain special characters.

Start Elasticsearch first

docker compose --env-file elk\.env -f elk\docker-compose.yaml up -d elasticsearch
docker compose --env-file elk\.env -f elk\docker-compose.yaml ps

Set the passwords

On a brand-new data volume, ELASTIC_PASSWORD becomes the initial password. On an existing volume, changing the variable does nothing, so reset the passwords explicitly and copy exactly what you enter into .env:

docker exec -it elasticsearch bin/elasticsearch-reset-password -u elastic -i
docker exec -it elasticsearch bin/elasticsearch-reset-password -u kibana_system -i

elastic is the admin account: you sign in to Kibana with it and Logstash writes with it in this local setup. kibana_system is only the account Kibana uses to talk to Elasticsearch; you never log in with it.

Start Logstash and Kibana

docker compose --env-file elk\.env -f elk\docker-compose.yaml up -d logstash kibana
# if they were already running before the password change:
docker compose --env-file elk\.env -f elk\docker-compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate logstash kibana
ServiceAddressPurpose
Elasticsearchhttp://localhost:9200Stores and searches logs
Kibanahttp://localhost:5601UI and dashboards
Logstash APIhttp://localhost:9600Pipeline status
Logstash Beats inputlocalhost:5044Reserved, unused

Watch each container with docker logs -f elasticsearch (or logstash, kibana). Logstash prints every parsed event (rubydebug) with a service field, so you can confirm parsing works. A Kibana error unable to authenticate user [kibana_system] means the password in .env does not match Elasticsearch.

5. Step 3: your logstash.conf and docker-compose.yaml explained

logstash.conf

input {
  file {
    path => ["/logs/*/*.log"]
    start_position => "beginning"
    sincedb_path => "/usr/share/logstash/data/logstash-sincedb"
    ecs_compatibility => "disabled"
    codec => multiline {
      pattern => "^\d{2}-\d{2}-\d{4} "
      negate => true
      what => "previous"
      auto_flush_interval => 2
    }
  }
}
filter {
  grok { match => { "message" => "^(?<log_timestamp>\d{2}-\d{2}-\d{4} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}\.\d{3}) \[%{DATA:thread}\] \[%{DATA:trace_context}\] %{LOGLEVEL:level}\s+%{GREEDYDATA:log_message}$" } }
  date { match => ["log_timestamp", "dd-MM-yyyy HH:mm:ss.SSS"]  timezone => "Asia/Kolkata"  target => "@timestamp" }
  grok { match => { "path" => "^/logs/(?<service>[^/]+)/" } }
  mutate { remove_field => ["log_timestamp"] }
}
output {
  elasticsearch {
    hosts => ["http://elasticsearch:9200"]
    user => "elastic"
    password => "${ELASTIC_PASSWORD}"
    index => "spring-logs-%{+YYYY.MM.dd}"
  }
  stdout { codec => rubydebug }
}
SettingWhat it does
pathWatches every .log in every service folder under /logs. New lines are picked up continuously, and new files and folders are discovered automatically.
start_position => "beginning"A file seen for the first time is read from its first line, so existing history is ingested.
sincedb_pathA bookmark file recording how far each log file has been read, so a restart continues instead of re-reading.
ecs_compatibility => "disabled"Keeps the classic field names path and host (the ones in your Discover sidebar). The grok on path below depends on this.
multilineA line that does not start with dd-MM-yyyy belongs to the previous event, so a stack trace stays in one document. auto_flush_interval => 2 emits the last event after 2 idle seconds; without it the newest line would wait for the next line to arrive.
grok on messageSplits the line into log_timestamp, thread, trace_context (traceId-spanId), level and log_message. It mirrors the logback pattern. Because there is no separate logger capture, log_message starts with service-logger.method - followed by the text.
dateParses the log time as India time and stores it in @timestamp (stored in UTC), so charts use when the event happened, not when it was ingested.
grok on pathTakes the folder name after /logs/ as service: api-gateway, order-service or inventory-service.
mutate remove_fieldDrops the temporary log_timestamp once it has been used.
elasticsearch outputSends to elasticsearch:9200 (the Docker service name) as elastic. ${ELASTIC_PASSWORD} is read from the container's environment. %{+YYYY.MM.dd} creates one index per day.
stdout rubydebugPrints each event in docker logs logstash, handy while testing; remove it later to cut noise.

docker-compose.yaml

ServiceKey lines
elasticsearchdiscovery.type: single-node skips cluster formation. xpack.security.enabled: "true" turns on logins. ELASTIC_PASSWORD sets the initial elastic password on a new volume. Heap is fixed at 512 MB. The named volume elasticsearch-data keeps your indexes across restarts and down.
logstashMounts your logstash.conf as the pipeline and ../logs read-only at /logs. It receives ELASTIC_PASSWORD as an environment variable. Ports 9600 (status API) and 5044 (unused Beats input) are published.
kibanaConnects to Elasticsearch as kibana_system with KIBANA_SYSTEM_PASSWORD. You log in to the UI as elastic, not this account.
all${VAR:?message} makes Compose stop with that message if the variable is missing from .env. depends_on only controls start order, not readiness; Logstash retries until Elasticsearch is up.
Two things to fix.
1. Duplicate logs after recreating Logstash. The sincedb lives inside the container, and no volume stores it. restart keeps it, but down followed by up, or --force-recreate (which the README suggests after a password change), loses it. With start_position => "beginning" every log file is then read again and indexed a second time. Persist it:
  logstash:
    volumes:
      - logstash-data:/usr/share/logstash/data
volumes:
  logstash-data:
2. Stack traces are cut in log_message. As written, GREEDYDATA stops at the first newline, so log_message holds only the first line of a multi-line event; the full text, trace included, is still in message. To keep it all in log_message, end the grok with (?<log_message>(?m).*) instead of %{GREEDYDATA:log_message}.

6. Step 4: confirm the index exists

In Kibana, open Dev Tools, then Console, and run GET _cat/indices.

  • The index shows yellow because it has 1 primary and 1 replica shard, and a single-node cluster has nowhere to put the replica. That is normal locally; for production add nodes or set replicas as needed.
  • The docs count in the screenshot is 388 events.
  • The index is named .03 although the logs are from 4 October: the daily name uses @timestamp in UTC, and 00:11 in India time is still 3 October in UTC.

7. Step 5: explore in Kibana

Sign in and create the data view

Open http://localhost:5601 and sign in with username elastic and the password you set with the docker command. Go to Analytics, Discover, Create data view, then fill in:

  • Name: ecommerce-logs
  • Index pattern: spring-logs-* (the right panel confirms how many indexes match)
  • Timestamp field: @timestamp

Discover: search the raw logs

Useful KQL queries in the search bar:

service : "order-service" and level : "ERROR"
service : "inventory-service" and log_message : *unavailable*
level.keyword : "INFO" and not service : "api-gateway"

Top values of a field

Visualize: counts per service

Follow one request across services with its trace

Copy the traceId from any log line and paste it into the search bar. Every line from every service that handled that request comes back, in time order.

8. Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely cause and fix
Discover is emptyWiden the time range; confirm the index exists with GET _cat/indices.
No index at allLogstash sees no files. Check that logs/<service>/*.log exist and are mounted at /logs, then read docker logs logstash.
Fields missing or _grokparsefailure tagThe log pattern and the grok pattern no longer match. Compare them.
Kibana cannot authenticateKIBANA_SYSTEM_PASSWORD differs from Elasticsearch. Reset it, update .env, recreate the container.
Duplicate documentsLogstash was recreated and lost its sincedb, so files were re-read. Persist /usr/share/logstash/data in a volume (section 5).
Wrong day in index nameIndex dates use UTC; see section 6.

9. Before going beyond local

  • Turn on TLS for Elasticsearch; the README notes security is on but HTTP is not encrypted.
  • Give Logstash its own role and user instead of elastic.
  • Add Filebeat on each host and switch Logstash to the Beats input (5044) so Logstash no longer needs file access.
  • Add index lifecycle management to delete old daily indexes, and run more than one Elasticsearch node.
